For Beckett devotees, this Godot will come across as both idiosyncratic and faithful, a weird masterwork seen and heard afresh.

Back in New York with a starry cast, Waiting for Godot makes you think about meaning in an indifferent world, and that’s a timely takeaway.
It's not Godot at its most evocative, but the delight of Reeves and Winter onstage together, bouncing off each other as easily as they did in '89, is worth a watch.
Reeves and Winter may not save the world this time, but their endless adventure in Beckett’s wasteland is a strange, curious, and surprisingly affecting experiment.
Lloyd's revival of Waiting for Godot effectively does just that, framing the play less as linear drama than as something more akin to a multi-movement piece of instrumental music.
The "Matrix" actor suffers beautifully in his Broadway debut, although it's the revelatory Winter who will haunt you long after the curtain falls.
It's a relatively straightforward Waiting for Godot that's performed at an impressive clip and mostly lands the important beats.

Reeves, Winter, and Lloyd have not produced a revolutionary or revelatory Godot (you’re still grateful to inhale the night air when Beckett’s existential trudge is done), but they have found a route to a non-disastrous, pleasurable one.
It is not a performance, and Reeves very studied and mannered delivery of his lines is enough to ban the word “staccato” from Webster’s.
But I would have rather spent a longer time with a Godot helmed by a director more concerned about what he wanted to say than how differently he could say it.
But they don’t come close to truly conveying the characters’ existential despair, nor their vaudevillian-style clowning.
Each actor seems left on his own.
Lloyd's production succeeds not by updating Beckett or making the play more palatable, but by trusting that seventy years later, the waiting has only intensified.
Reeves is stiff and awkward in a role that requires more of a lithe comic presence.

Despite the shortcomings of the leads’ muted performances and some questionable directorial choices, this Godot does have a comic energy and conveys a hint of Beckett’s bleak vision of humanity’s eternal quandary in seeking meaning where none seems to exist.
Here, the pair’s well-meaning performances, combined with Beckett’s ultra-dense text, end up being far more successful at periodically boring us than delighting us.
“Waiting for Godot” was subpar, forgettable, and dull.

It is, nevertheless, sheer folly to build a revival of Godot, one of the most challenging plays in twentieth-century drama, on a pair of actors with little theatrical experience and limited technical skills.
